text.Système d'expression propre non directem: A distinct system of expression not directly intelligible to speakers of another language.
text.Variante locale d'une même langue, intel: A local variant of the same language, intelligible with a little effort. E.g.: bulu, ewondo, eton, mangisa → Beti-Fang language.
text.Langue d'une ethnie faisant partie d'une: The language of an ethnic group that is part of a nation, not extending beyond the borders of a State (ACA LAN).
text.Premier moyen d'expression acquis pendan: The first means of expression acquired in childhood, through which the child is socialised.
text.Langue servant à la communication entre: A language used for communication between different language communities. E.g.: Pidgin English (NW/SW), Fulfulde (North).
text.Langue parlée de part et d'autre de deux: A language spoken on both sides of the border between two neighbouring countries (e.g. Fulfulde, Gbaya, Tupuri).

text.Réseau de 51 communautés : relations his: Network of 51 communities: historical, linguistic, geographical, social and cognitive relations.
text.Peuple majoritaire et largement autochto: The majority and largely autochthonous people of the Menoua, neighbouring Baleveng, Bafoussam and Mbouda, the Bafou speak Yemba. The chiefdom relies on the colleges of the “9” and the “7” notables, ritual societies and a rich cult of skulls; farming, livestock and trade sustain the community, which celebrates its Lemou festival every two years.
text.« ceux qui fouillent jusqu'au fond », qu: “those who dig down to the bottom”, who go in depth
text.Peuple forestier minoritaire, mobile et: A minority forest people, mobile and egalitarian, the Baka live alongside the Nzimé and the Mpoupieng, from Yokadouma to Lomié and as far as Bipindi. Hunting, gathering, fishing and small-scale farming sustain a community where land is a common good and where the initiates of the jengi ensure justice and protection.
text.Les Adie (Bakoko) vivent autour d'Édéa,: The Adie (Bakoko) live around Édéa, mixed with the Basaa, the Bati-Mpoo and populations from elsewhere. Organised into two large families, the Benanes and the Dogtomèn, they combine fishing, hunting and farming on the banks of the Sanaga, and celebrate the Mpoo festival every year in December.
text.du nom de l'ancêtre fondateur Adie ; lié: named after the founding ancestor Adie; linked to the name of Édéa
text.Venus de Ndiki (Mbam) par l'Ouest et Mak: Having come from Ndiki (Mbam) via the West and Makombé, the Banen Ndogtuna found in Yabassi a land of welcome where they live alongside the Bandem, Basaa, Bamiléké, Hausa, Bamoun, Beti, Bodiman and Dibum. Organised in hereditary chiefdoms, they live from farming, fishing and hunting, and celebrate the Ngankam every year in April.
text.Les Mboum, fondateurs historiques de Nga: The Mboum, historical founders of Ngaoundéré, are now a minority there among the Fulani, Gbaya, Hausa, Kanuri and migrants from the South. Strongly Islamised, patrilineal and organised around the chiefdom and the trade guilds, they practise farming, livestock rearing and an ancient craft tradition, to the rhythm of the tam-tam and the balafon.
text.Ngaoundéré renvoie à la montagne « au no: Ngaoundéré refers to the mountain “with a navel”, which gave the town its name
text.Les Peuls Walarbe de Gashiga, majoritair: The Fulani Walarbe of Gashiga, the majority in their area, live alongside the Fali and the Bata. Coming from Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger via Bashéo, Demsa and the Mandara Mountains, they form a hereditary lamidat where Islam governs social life; livestock rearing, farming, trade and Koranic teaching are its pillars.
text.Peuple de tradition guerrière et de chas: A people with a warrior tradition and of hunters, present in several regions of Cameroon and as far as the Central African Republic, Sudan and Nigeria, the Gbaya live here alongside the Makaa of the North, the Bobilis, the Kpere, the Kako and the Bamvələ. Initiation into the labi once structured social life; today largely Christianised, they remain attached to traditional remedies and maize beer.
text.Venus du Soudan par Gudur et Mokong, les: Having come from Sudan via Gudur and Mokong, the Guiziga of Muturwa live among the Gudur and the Guidar, in a landscape of sacred mountains such as the “Finger of God”. Patrilineal, formerly organised under the authority of the lulo into classes of blacksmiths and cultivators, they honour their ancestors through the mulvring and celebrate the great festivals of Diguila and Muvulgum.
text.Fondateurs de Kousseri et gardiens de se: Founders of Kousseri and guardians of its traditions, the Kotoko (Mantagé) say they are descended from the Sao, who came from ancient Egypt via Sudan and Chad. Under the authority of a sultan surrounded by notables, this people of Logone fishermen honours the water spirits, builds dugout canoes and dances to the sound of the sultan's drums.
text.Majoritaires sur le plateau de Nkambe, l: In the majority on the Nkambe plateau, the Wimbum arrived there from the Tikar region, in search of fertile land and to escape Fulani raids. The sacred kingship of the fon, powerful secret societies, weaving, palm wine and maize beer characterise a culture close to those of the North-West and the West.
text.Majoritaires à Kolofata, les Kanuri y vi: In the majority in Kolofata, the Kanuri live there with the Mandara, Podoko, Mouktélé, Gamergou, Shuwa Arabs and Fulani. Coming from Yemen via Kouka and Maiduguri, these heirs of Bornu organise their lives around kingship, Islam and occupational castes (blacksmiths, butchers, weavers, tailors); farming, small livestock rearing and trade provide their living.
text.Majoritaires et autochtones autour de Mo: In the majority and indigenous around Mora, the Wandala founded an ancient sultanate, open to the Kanuri, Podoko, Mouktélé, Shuwa Arabs, Malgwa and Kotoko. Islamised, and organised into kingship, castes and age groups, they live from farming, livestock rearing, trade and crafts, and share a long migratory route with the Kanuri.
text.Majoritaires autour de Kaélé (« près de: In the majority around Kaélé (“near the water”), the Moundang live alongside the Guiziga, Fulani and Toupouri. Coming from Sudan via Léré, in Chad, with which they share festivals, initiation and kingship, they obey a sovereign, the gon, surrounded by eleven notables. The guinarou, a great male initiation, and the biennial Gbeza festival punctuate their lives.
text.Petit groupe forestier de l'Est, les Mpo: A small forest group of the East, the Mpoupieng live mixed with the Baka, the Maka and the Djem, whose language they often speak. Their society, little hierarchical, grants prestige to the prosperous head of family; cash-crop and subsistence farming, palm wine and the balafon mark their life.
text.Peuple majoritaire des Bamboutos, les Ba: The majority people of the Bamboutos, the Babadjou (Mbasso) speak ngomba'e, a language specific to the grouping. Most of them came from Bapa (North-West), and are organised around the paramount chief, the colleges of the 9 and the 7 notables and ritual servants; coffee, livestock and subsistence crops sustain them, and the Lehere festival closes each year.
text.Les Mvón-Mvón disent avoir toujours vécu: The Mvón-Mvón say they have always lived in Yokadouma, where they live alongside the Mbimo, Bayege, Gbaya and Kako. Organised around kinship and a hereditary power exercised by consensus, they live from farming, hunting, fishing and gathering; labi and patenge set the rhythm of their ceremonies.
text.Les Ŋgóló, l'un des clans du peuple Orok: The Ŋgóló, one of the clans of the Oroko people, live in good harmony with their neighbours and with the migrants from the Grassfields whom they call báŋgárà. Coming from Ísàkà (Bakassi) via Màtùbà, they have a loosely centralised chiefdom and a sacred house, the étánà, which preserves the culture of the village; coffee, food crops, hunting and livestock rearing provide their living.
text.Peuple de montagne des monts Mandara, lo: A mountain people of the Mandara mountains, long turned in on itself, the Podoko (Parkwa) say they came from Gaza by way of Waza and the Logone. The mountains, their cradle and refuge, shelter their sacred places; millet and bean farming, small livestock rearing and smithing sustain them, and the festivals of Dilda and of the harvests mark the year.
text.Fondé en 1394 par Nchare Yen, un prince: Founded in 1394 by Nchare Yen, a Tikar prince from Rifoum (Mbankim), the Bamoun kingdom is ruled by a mfon surrounded by notables, servants and the royal family. Shüpamom, the language of the Mbèn subjugated by the founder, became the language of the kingdom. Fine crafts, the cult of the dead and the great Nguon festival make Foumban famous.
text.Les Djo de Bandjoun forment une grande c: The Djo of Bandjoun form a large chiefdom of the West, descended from peoples who came from Ŋwa (Haut-Nkam), Baleng and the Bamoun country. Kingship, brotherhoods and the skull cult structure society; coffee, trade and crafts (forging, basketry, sculpture) sustain it, and the Msəm Tódjom festival brings the community together in odd-numbered years.
text.« ceux qui achètent », ceux qui ont de l: “those who buy”, those who have money
text.Majoritaires dans leur canton, les Bafia: In the majority in their canton, the Bafia of Rigama live alongside Bamiléké, Tikar, Hausa and Yambassa in a spirit of living together. Descended from Bakoa (Bokito), they descend from Meden to Ngam, “son of Ngam”. Farmers, basket-makers and sculptors, they dance the dom at the funerals of elders and exhibit their art at the Mbam Art festival.
text.Majoritaires dans leur zone du Ndé, les: A majority in their area of the Ndé, the Balengou are related to the Baleng, with whom they share political rites, and live in contact with Bamena, Baïok, Bangwa, Bafang and Mbouda. The chiefdom, the notables and the social classes (royal family, blacksmiths, craftsmen) structure a society in which the ancestors are honoured and where the mbouob festival brings the community together.
text.Les Bamvələ vivent sur leur terre ancest: The Bamvələ live on their ancestral land, forming the majority among the Gbaya, the Makaa and newcomers. An open society in which the chief decides in assembly with his notables, they practise farming, fishing and a little trade, share dance and the mvet with the Beti, and make mbɔ̀l their emblematic dish.
text.Les Ndog-Bacek forment le noyau majorita: The Ndog-Bacek form the majority core of a Basaa group that has absorbed several neighbouring groups (Lìmùù, Liŋgɔ̀k, Mbamndân), who adopted Bàsàa. Settled on their ancestral land after a migration that set out from Ŋgɔk-Lituɓa, they live mainly from cocoa, the oil palm and bananas, in a patrilineal society where decisions are taken by consensus.
text.Majoritaires dans leur groupement, au co: In the majority in their grouping, in contact with the Ngoe and the Esse, the Bulu of Yekombo live from cocoa, food crops, fishing and basketry. Societies of families and hierarchical chiefdoms, they used to gather under the adum tree to consult the ancestors; Christianity has replaced these cults, but the cuisine, the eɲəŋə dance and the bikutsi remain.
text.Les Edingding (Mengara), l'un des grands: The Edingding (Mengara), one of the great Éton lineages of the Lékié, neighbour the Medoum, Batchenga, Mvele and Mvog-Beloa. Coming from the other bank of the Sanaga via Emana, Talla, Saa and Elig-Fomo, they acquired their lands through friendship. An egalitarian and hospitable society, they grow cocoa and dance the bikutsi.
text.nom d'un arbre ; pour les voisins, le no: name of a tree; for the neighbours, the name of a great warrior
text.Au cœur de Yaoundé, Efoulan se décrit co: In the heart of Yaoundé, Efoulan describes itself as a “mixture of peoples”: the Ewondo live there with Basaa, people from the Grassfields and from the North. Like all the Beti, they say they crossed the Sanaga on the back of a mythical snake. Catholic and highly urbanised, they keep the olugu, respect for elders, and the music of the balafon and the tam-tam.
text.Majoritaires dans leur localité de Zoété: In the majority in their locality of Zoétélé, the Foŋ live alongside the Esə, Ŋdoŋ and Jəmdək, all Bulu. Like the other Beti, they say they came from the other bank of the Sanaga. Organised around kinship and inherited specialisms (dancers, hunters, carpenters), they live from cocoa, timber and cassava sticks, and dance the eɲəŋgə to the sound of the mvet.
text.Les Esaɲan de Minko'o, Fang majoritaires: The Esaɲan of Minko'o, a Fang majority in their area, live alongside the Bulu, the Zaman and the Baka. Their language extends from Océan and Vallée-du-Ntem to northern Gabon and Congo. Cocoa, livestock, hunting and bushmeat with plantain make up their daily life; every 1 January, the visit to the graves brings the whole village together.
text.« ceux de Ɲan », les enfants de Ɲan: “those of Ɲan”, the children of Ɲan
text.Les Ndog-Banɔl, que leurs voisins appell: The Ndog-Banɔl, whom their neighbours call Fɔmbɔ, form a small group of 21 villages, bordering the Inoubou-Nord canton, the Alinga, the Basaa of Sanaga-Maritime, the Ndog-Biakat and the Yengui. Settled on a land of welcome, a former military camp, they live from cocoa, food crops and gathering.
text.les villages issus de l'ancêtre Banɔl: the villages descended from the ancestor Banɔl
text.Petit peuple sawa de pêcheurs, les Malim: A small Sawa people of fishermen, the Malimba say they are descended from Elimbe, son of Bendi, the ancestor who came from the Congo. Settled along the Sanaga and the ocean, between Dizangué and Logasse, alongside the Duala, Bakoko, Banen and Babimbi, they honour the water spirits through the jengu and celebrate the ihangabinde every year.
text.les enfants de l'ancêtre Elimbe: the children of the ancestor Elimbe
text.Le canton Ebombo, douze villages manguis: The Ebombo canton, twelve Manguissa villages, lives in harmony with the Engba grouping, the Begnia Bega, the people of the Sanaga and the Saa canton, and welcomes Hausa, people from Bamenda, Bamiléké and Malians. Having come, like the other Beti, from the other bank of the Sanaga, the Manguissa grow cocoa, groundnut and cucumber and every year initiate their young people into the minken mimbon dance.
text.Premiers occupants du département qui po: The first occupants of the department that bears their name, the Mbéré live in small numbers among the Bororo and the Fulani, whose language they mainly speak. Strongly Islamised, they are renowned as masters of honey and as healers; farming, rearing of goats and sheep and pottery complete their activities.
text.Les Kwasio, Mvumbo (Ngoumba) et Mabi (Ma: The Kwasio, Mvumbo (Ngoumba) and Mabi (Mabea) live in the Kribi region alongside the Batanga, Bulu, Fang and Yasa, with relatives in Gabon and Equatorial Guinea. Fishing, hunting and the cultivation of cassava, plantain and cocoyam sustain them; the Ngúmá màɓi and M̀pfúl Mvumbɔ festivals celebrate their identity.
text.Mvumbo vient du tronc de l'arbre sìó ; K: Mvumbo comes from the trunk of the sìó tree; Kwàsíó, “having hollowed out the sìó trunk”
text.Les Biatsota, Mvele de Ntui, vivent en b: The Biatsota, Mvele of Ntui, live in good neighbourliness with the Djané, Nkulutu and Biindandjengué, and speak Ossananga, whose speakers are found as far as the edges of Adamawa. Catholics for a long time, they live from cocoa, fishing, trade and food crops, and share many customs with the Eton.
text.Peuple de grands guerriers venu de l'Ada: A people of great warriors who came from Adamawa, the Vute (Babute) conquered their lands by crossing the Sanaga near Mbandjock, and today neighbour the Eton, the Mbamois, the Nanga, the Yezoum and the Mvele. A hereditary chiefdom, hunting, fishing and farming, cassava couscous and the war dance to the djiiŋ drum characterise them.
text.Majoritaires dans l'arrondissement de Le: In the majority in the Lembe-Yezoum subdivision, the Yezoum, who came from Adamawa, live alongside the Vute, Yebekolo, Nanga, Mvele, Eton and Mbamois. Their dynastic chiefdom is held by the great Angoula family. Trade, cash and food crops, basketry and the making of musical instruments provide their living; their culture and language are close to those of the Ewondo.
text.Fondé par un chasseur en quête de terres: Founded by a hunter in search of land, the Bamoungoum kingdom, the majority in its area, welcomes Hausa, people from Mbouda, Bansoa and Bamoun. A chiefdom structured around notables and protective secret societies, ancestor and skull worship, the refuge cave of Ndə nə kaŋ nsaŋ: every two years, for four months, the Bamoungoum celebrate their great festival Nə kaŋ pə Muŋgum.
text.Peuple de pêcheurs de la côte de Kribi,: A fishing people of the Kribi coast, the Batanga came along the coast from the Nigeria-Cameroon border and keep ties with ndà-speaking peoples of Gabon, Equatorial Guinea and beyond. A minority among the Mabea, Bulu, Bakoko and Yasa, they live to the rhythm of the sea, the water spirits and the Mayi festival, which commemorates the return from exile in 1916.
text.Les Lagwane, Kotoko du sultanat de Logon: The Lagwane, Kotoko of the sultanate of Logone-Birni, live from fishing and farming along the Logone, in symbiosis with the Massa, Mousgoum, Arabs and Kanuri. Heirs of the Sao, who came from Yemen via Sudan, Kanem-Bornu and Baguirmi, they honour the water goddess before the great fishing expeditions and dance the kounkouli when the sultan goes out.
text.Minoritaires à Garoua, les Arabes Choa v: A minority in Garoua, the Shuwa Arabs live among the Fali, Guiziga, Bata and Fulani, with whom they share Fulfulde. Arriving three centuries ago from Ouaddaï (Abéché, Chad) via Mora, they have made their three-hundred-year-old mosque and the chiefdom their places of memory. Small-scale trade, tontines and catering occupy the women; milk and the sorghum ball are at the heart of the cuisine.
text.Majoritaires à Meiganga, où ils côtoient: In the majority in Meiganga, where they live alongside the Toupouri, Bororo, Bamiléké and Hausa, the Baya (Bouforo) belong to the large Gbaya group that extends from Sudan and the Central African Republic to the Congo and Nigeria. An egalitarian society yet attached to respect, they grow cassava, maize, potato, beans and yam, and the labi school, a genuine training of warriors, remains at the heart of their education.
text.évoque des interdits alimentaires liés à: evokes food taboos linked to meat
text.Majoritaires dans le lamidat de Mbé, les: In the majority in the lamidate of Mbé, the Dii live with Fulani, Moundang, Toupouri, Mada, Mafa and Bamiléké. Coming from Mayo-Rey, they found a place of refuge in Mbé. The chiefdom, the circumciser-priest and the blacksmith organise society; circumcision, with its three-day mbé dance, is its great rite.
text.La chefferie de Fondjenti réunit des Ntî: The Fondjenti chiefdom brings together Ntî from Bamwa, the Fondonti and the Bapoutchis found on the spot; all speak Nufi. A dynastic monarchy, deliberating brotherhoods, skull worship and the sacred place of the palm, “the tree that gives everything”, characterise this people, proud of their exogamy and hospitality.
text.Peuple des Hauts-Plateaux, les Bapa (Pep: A people of the Hauts-Plateaux, the Bapa (Pepa) settled on a rugged site never occupied before them, rich in waterfalls, caves and sacred forests. A hereditary chiefdom linked to sister chiefdoms such as Batié, a cult of skulls and ancestors, and the great biennial kan festival, where young boys are initiated and shape their identity.
text.Les Maka Bebend forment un clan maka rel: The Maka Bebend form a relatively isolated Maka clan but one linked to the other Maka groups of the East and to the Ngoumba of the South. Having come from Adamawa in the 17th century with the Maka Bwanz and Maka Ebe, they live from farming, hunting, fishing and crafts, and dance the mpiné around the fire, formerly on returning from war.
text.Petit peuple sawa des rives du Wouri, le: A small Sawa people of the banks of the Wouri, the Bodiman live among the Ewodi, Duala, Banen and Basaa of Yabassi, whose languages they speak. Having come from the Congo, as fishermen and farmers, they have the dugout canoe, the paddle and the crocodile as symbols, and every December celebrate the Suunɛm Ebanabamboa, which has become the festival of the Bodiman canton.
text.Majoritaires dans leur zone, les Toupour: In the majority in their area, the Toupouri, long very isolated, now live alongside the Fulani and Moundang. Having come from Sudan through Chad, with which they live “in absolute fraternity”, they organise their society around the doore (land chiefs), clan notables and maagay initiates. Farming, livestock, bil-bil and pottery are their livelihood, and the cockerel festival, the feo kake, opens the new year every October.
text.Majoritaires à Guidiguis, où ils vivent: In the majority in Guidiguis, where they live with the Toupouri, the Fulani speak Fulfulde, a language widespread from Senegal to Cameroon. Coming from Mali via Nigeria and Guinea, they are organised in a lamidate (lamido, kaigama, kofa) and have deeply shaped their culture on Islam; livestock rearing, trade and the sale of milk provide their living.
text.Les Kali de Bèlèl, peuple de langue mbou: The Kali of Bèlèl, a Mboum-speaking people, live as a minority among the Fulani, Dourou, Hausa, Beti, Basaa, Toupouri and Bamiléké. Having come from Mayo-Rey (Lugéré Baka) via Mbang, they keep a family chiefdom and live from farming and trade. The dzwùŋ dance accompanies circumcisions, millet threshing and funerals, and the millet festival, held twice a year, drives away disease.
text.Majoritaires dans leur zone, les Pɛrɛ vi: In the majority in their area, the Pɛrɛ live with the Mboum, Hausa, Gbaya and Fulani, whose languages they often speak. Coming from Gañe in Nigeria via Gɛŋfəlabo and Almé, they have matrilineal kinship, a chief and kings, and celebrate the mburi in March to call down blessing. Farming, trade and varied crafts provide their living.
